4855-history-of-the-united-netherlands-1:
In early 1588 the Dutch republic lives under the shadow of invasion, and John Lothrop Motley follows English commissioners sent to sound out peace. Willoughby reluctantly takes command, Cecil tours a desolated Flanders with Dale, and Dr. Rogers holds long interviews with Parma, touched by the duke's courtesy.

Parma speaks fervently for peace, yet the queen distrusts her own envoy's credulity, and the commissioners' hopes rest on flattery and harangue. Motley sets their optimism against the ruined countryside they travel through. Readers see a peace mission that revealed more about Spanish deception than about any real path to settlement.
history-of-the-united-netherlands-1588a:
The first part of chapter eighteen in John Lothrop Motley's History of the United Netherlands surveys the dread year 1588. Prophecies as to the year fill the opening, with the distracted condition of the Dutch provinces. England's Queen quarrels with her wisest statesmen over their course of action. Dutch leaders and their English governor are in deadly feud.

Motley calls the winter before the Armada the darkest that ever fell on the Netherlands. It disappointed the more because it succeeded a period of comparative prosperity and triumph. Leicester's resignation, Parma's preparations, and Spain's fleet approach together. This portion is all approach and omen, the held breath of the history. Motley's structure makes the reader share the waiting. Deliverance, when it comes in the next part, has been earned by dread.
uslaw-usc-t2-s158a:
Section 158a of Title 2 of the United States Code covers gifts of money or securities to the Library of Congress. It sits in Chapter 5 of that title, on the Library of Congress. The section deals with cases where quick action is needed. That need may arise from terms set by the donor or from like factors.

In such a case the Librarian of Congress may take temporary possession of the gift. That step is subject to approval under section 156 of the title. The gift is to be receipted for and invested, reinvested, or retained as section 157 provides. The text then sets out an exception for a gift of securities. The text is current through Public Law 119-134.
uslaw-usc-t2-s1868a:
Section 1868a of Title 2 of the United States Code covers reports of disbursements by the Architect of the Capitol. It sits in Chapter 28 of that title, in the part on appropriations and spending. Part (a) states when reports are due. Not later than sixty days after the last day of each half-year span, the Architect must send Congress a report.

The report must be a detailed, itemized account of the disbursements for the work of that office in the span. Part (b) states what the report must take in. The first item named is the name of each person who takes a payment, as the list goes on. The text is current through Public Law 119-134.
uslaw-usc-t2-s28a:
Section 28a of Title 2 of the United States Code covers the Compilation of the Precedents of the House of Representatives. It sits in Chapter 2 of that title, on the organization of Congress. The Speaker is cleared and directed to complete that work by 1 January 1977. He is also to prepare an updated set of those precedents each two years after that date.

Copies of the Compilation are to be printed in a count large enough for broad use. The copies must be at hand for each Member of the House and for its standing committees, as the text states. The title of the section also covers the printing and supply of copies in its scope. The text is current through Public Law 119-134.
uslaw-usc-t2-s658a:
Section 658a of Title 2 of the United States Code lists exclusions from its part on federal mandates. It sits in Chapter 17A of that title, on congressional budget matters, in the part on federal mandates. The part is stated not to apply to a set of provisions. The provisions may stand in a bill, joint resolution, amendment, motion, or conference report before Congress.

The first provision carved out is one that enforces the rights of individuals under the Constitution. The second covers provisions that set up or enforce rights that bar bias. The grounds of bias named are race, color, religion, sex, national origin, age, handicap, or disability. The third covers provisions that call for compliance with accounting rules, as the list goes on. The text is current through Public Law 119-134.
